title: Academic vs General Training Reading
summary: Same 40 questions, same 60 minutes, same question types — yet the two versions of IELTS Reading are marked on different scales and taken for completely different reasons. Here's how to tell which one you actually need and what changes once you sit down.

seo.title: IELTS Academic vs General Reading Explained | Vidaara
seo.description: IELTS Academic vs General Training Reading: passages, sources, scoring differences and which test you need for university, work or migration — free guide.

objectives: Explain the difference in passages and text sources between Academic and General Training Reading
Decide which version of the test you actually need for your goal
Explain why General Training needs more correct answers for the same band
Adjust your section pacing to match the difficulty curve of each version

blocks.html:
People often assume Academic Reading is "harder" and General Training is "easier". That's only half true, and the half that's false costs candidates marks. The question types are identical — Matching Headings, True/False/Not Given, sentence completion, and the rest all appear in both. What differs is the reading material and, more quietly, the marking scale. A General Training candidate who coasts through the easy early texts can still miss their band because GT demands more correct answers.

Before anything else, one point that trips up first-timers: you don't get to pick freely. The version you sit is fixed by why you're taking IELTS. Get that wrong and you can be forced to resit. So let's start there.

Which one do you actually need?

Your purpose decides your test, not your preference. The dividing line is roughly "study or professional registration" versus "migration, work, or school".

  • Academic — undergraduate and postgraduate university admission, and professional registration bodies (medicine, nursing, engineering, accountancy). If an institution is assessing whether you can cope with academic English, it wants Academic.
  • General Training — migration to countries like Australia, Canada, the UK and New Zealand; work or training below degree level; and secondary-school entry. Most permanent-residence and skilled-worker visa streams accept GT.

The catch: some professional and immigration pathways have their own rule, and a few universities will accept GT for certain programmes. Always confirm the exact requirement with the receiving organisation — the visa office, the university admissions page, the licensing board — before you book. A wasted test fee and a five-week wait for a resit is a painful way to learn this.

blocks.title: Check the requirement in writing, not in a forum
blocks.html: The single most expensive mistake here is booking the wrong module because "someone online said GT was fine". Requirements vary by country, visa stream and even the year. Verify on the official body's own page — IELTS.org, plus your destination's immigration or admissions site — and keep a screenshot of the requirement you're meeting.

What's inside each version

Both tests run 60 minutes and have 40 questions worth one mark each. The structure of the reading material is where they part ways.

Academic

Three long passages, roughly 2,150–2,750 words in total, taken from books, journals, newspapers and magazines. They're written for a general, educated audience — you are not expected to have specialist knowledge of the topic. Diagrams or glossaries appear if a passage uses technical terms. The three passages are broadly similar in difficulty rather than ramping up sharply.

General Training

Three sections that climb in difficulty:

  • Section 1 — "social survival". Two or three short, everyday texts: notices, advertisements, timetables, leaflets. Practical, factual information you'd meet living in an English-speaking country.
  • Section 2 — "workplace survival". Two work-related texts: job descriptions, contracts, staff handbooks, training materials, pay-and-conditions documents.
  • Section 3 — "general reading". One longer, more complex discursive passage on a topic of general interest, closer in style and difficulty to an Academic passage.

blocks.title: The skills you learn transfer both ways
blocks.html: Because the 40 question types are the same across both modules, every strategy lesson in this course — Matching Headings, True/False/Not Given and the rest — applies to you whichever version you sit. Only the practice passages differ. Whether you book through the British Council or IDP, the underlying test is the same.

The scoring twist nobody warns you about

Here's the non-obvious part. Both versions convert a raw score out of 40 into a band, but the conversion is not the same. Because GT texts are more everyday, you need more correct answers to hit the same band. For band 7, an Academic candidate needs roughly 30/40; a GT candidate needs about 34–35/40. That gap changes how you should play the test.

blocks.title: GT candidates: the easy start is a trap
blocks.html: On Academic, needing 30/40 for band 7 means you can afford ten wrong. On GT you can only miss five or six. The danger is that Section 1 feels almost too easy, so you rush it and drop marks on careless slips — a mis-spelled word in a completion answer, a missed "NOT GIVEN". Those slips are cheap on Academic and expensive on GT. Treat the short texts with the same care as the long one.

How pacing should differ

Because the difficulty curves are different, your timing plan should be too. On Academic the three passages are roughly level, so an even split works. On GT the load rises, so bank time early to protect the hard finish.

blocks.title: Pacing by version
items: Academic — roughly even. About 20 minutes per passage. If anything, give Passage 3 a touch more, since dense argument text can be slow.
GT Section 1 — move fast, about 12–15 minutes. The texts are short and factual. Answer accurately but don't linger; you're banking time.
GT Section 2 — about 18 minutes. Workplace documents can hide detail in dense clauses. Read the conditions carefully — this is where careless errors creep in.
GT Section 3 — protect 25+ minutes. This passage behaves like an Academic text. Don't let an overrun in Sections 1–2 eat into it.
Both versions — write answers on the sheet as you go. There is no transfer time in Reading, so a plan to "copy at the end" loses marks when the clock beats you.

blocks.title: Same day, same paper feel
blocks.html: Whichever module you sit, spelling and grammar count in Reading answers just as they do in Listening — a correct idea spelled wrong is marked wrong. This matters more on GT, where the tighter scoring gives you less room for slips.

faqs.q: Are the questions different in Academic and General Training Reading?
faqs.a: No. Both versions use exactly the same question types and both have 40 questions in 60 minutes. Only the texts differ — Academic uses long passages from books and journals, while General Training uses everyday and workplace texts plus one longer passage.

faqs.q: Which IELTS Reading test do I need?
faqs.a: Take Academic for university admission or professional registration, and General Training for migration, work below degree level, or secondary school. Always confirm the exact requirement with the university, visa office or licensing body before booking.

faqs.q: Why do I need more correct answers on General Training for the same band?
faqs.a: Because GT texts are more everyday and accessible, the marking scale demands a higher raw score for each band. For band 7 you need roughly 30/40 on Academic but about 34–35/40 on General Training.

faqs.q: Is General Training Reading easier than Academic?
faqs.a: The early texts are simpler, but the scoring is stricter, so it is not automatically easier to score well. The tighter conversion means careless mistakes on the short texts cost you more than the same slips would on Academic.
